Attention-deficit disorder is usually described as a deficit of attention, but Gabor Maté argues that the label conceals more than it explains. In *Scattered Minds*, he proposes that the characteristic distractibility is better understood as a developmental adaptation—a nervous system that learned, early and under stress, to tune out what it could not bear to tune in. This reframing matters because it shifts the question from what is wrong with the child to what happened in the child's environment.

## The Biology of Attention

It is important to note that Maté situates his argument within a robust neurobiological framework centred on the prefrontal cortex, a region responsible for regulating attention and impulse whose maturation unfolds predominantly in the postnatal period. Furthermore, the development of these neural circuits is profoundly influenced by the quality of emotional attunement provided by caregivers, and sustained exposure to stress within the caregiving context may significantly compromise their optimal formation. Consequently, behaviors that educators frequently interpret as defiance or a lack of motivation can be understood as the observable manifestation of a regulatory system deprived of essential developmental conditions.

Crucially, the argument does not assign causal responsibility to parents. Maté emphasizes that hereditary factors confer a heightened sensitivity, while environmental circumstances shape the ultimate expression of that sensitivity. This nuanced distinction serves to remove blame without diminishing responsibility.

## What Follows From This

If the disorder is an adaptation, medication can be useful but cannot be sufficient. The deeper work is to create, in adulthood, the relational conditions missing in childhood: patience, acceptance, and the experience of being attuned to. Maté describes this as self-parenting, and he is explicit that it is slow work unfolding over years rather than weeks.

The reframing does not make the problem smaller. It makes it more human, and suggests the most effective interventions treat the person as a whole rather than as a set of symptoms to be managed.
